prompt: In the city of Lincoln, there is an empty jail, at least two townspeople and at least one goon. A game proceeds over several days, starting with morning. Each morning, one randomly selected unjailed person is placed in jail. If at this point all goons are jailed, and at least one townsperson remains, then the townspeople win. If at this point all townspeople are jailed and at least one goon remains, then the goons win. Each evening, if there is at least one goon and at least one townsperson not in jail, then one randomly selected townsperson is jailed. If at this point there are at least as many goons remaining as townspeople remaining, then the goons win. The game ends immediately after any group wins. Find the probability that the townspeople win if there are initially two townspeople and one goon.

solutions.title: Only the first morning matters
solutions.body:
If the goon is jailed on the first morning (probability $\frac13$), all goons are jailed and two townspeople remain, so the townspeople win. Otherwise a townsperson is jailed in the morning, and in the evening the only remaining townsperson is jailed; then the remaining goon outnumbers the $0$ townspeople and the goons win. So the probability is $\frac13$.

**Answer: $\frac13$**

prompt: In the city of Lincoln, there is an empty jail, at least two townspeople and at least one goon. A game proceeds over several days, starting with morning. Each morning, one randomly selected unjailed person is placed in jail. If at this point all goons are jailed, and at least one townsperson remains, then the townspeople win. If at this point all townspeople are jailed and at least one goon remains, then the goons win. Each evening, if there is at least one goon and at least one townsperson not in jail, then one randomly selected townsperson is jailed. If at this point there are at least as many goons remaining as townspeople remaining, then the goons win. The game ends immediately after any group wins. Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that, if there are initially $2n$ townspeople and $1$ goon, then the probability the townspeople win is greater than $50\%$.

solutions.title: Probability the goon survives
solutions.body:
The goon wins exactly when he is never jailed in the mornings. Each day removes one townsperson in the morning and one in the evening, so the game lasts $n$ days. The goon avoids jail on all $n$ mornings with probability $\frac{2n}{2n+1}\cdot\frac{2n-2}{2n-1}\cdots\frac{2}{3}$.

For $n=2$: $\frac45\cdot\frac23=\frac8{15}>\frac12$, so the townspeople win with probability $\frac7{15}<\frac12$. For $n=3$: $\frac67\cdot\frac8{15}=\frac{16}{35}<\frac12$, so the townspeople win with probability $\frac{19}{35}>\frac12$. Hence $n=3$.

**Answer: 3**

prompt: In the city of Lincoln, there is an empty jail, at least two townspeople and at least one goon. A game proceeds over several days, starting with morning. Each morning, one randomly selected unjailed person is placed in jail. If at this point all goons are jailed, and at least one townsperson remains, then the townspeople win. If at this point all townspeople are jailed and at least one goon remains, then the goons win. Each evening, if there is at least one goon and at least one townsperson not in jail, then one randomly selected townsperson is jailed. If at this point there are at least as many goons remaining as townspeople remaining, then the goons win. The game ends immediately after any group wins. Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that, if there are initially $n+1$ townspeople and $n$ goons, then the probability the townspeople win is less than $1\%$.

solutions.title: Closed form for the winning probability
solutions.body:
Let $p_n$ be the probability that the townspeople win starting with $n+1$ townspeople and $n$ goons, with $p_0=1$. In the morning a goon is jailed with probability $\frac{n}{2n+1}$; the evening then jails a townsperson, leaving $n$ townspeople and $n-1$ goons, i.e. the situation for $n-1$. If instead a townsperson is jailed in the morning (probability $\frac{n+1}{2n+1}$), the evening jail leaves $n-1$ townspeople against $n$ goons and the goons win. Hence $p_n=\frac{n}{2n+1}p_{n-1}$, so $p_n=\frac{n!}{(2n+1)!!}$ where $(2n+1)!!=1\cdot3\cdot5\cdots(2n+1)$. This is decreasing in $n$.

$p_5=\frac{5!}{3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9\cdot11}=\frac{8}{693}\approx0.01154>0.01$ and $p_6=\frac{6}{13}p_5=\frac{48}{9009}\approx0.00533<0.01$. So the smallest $n$ is $6$.

**Answer: 6**

prompt: In the city of Lincoln, there is an empty jail, at least two townspeople and at least one goon. A game proceeds over several days, starting with morning. Each morning, one randomly selected unjailed person is placed in jail. If at this point all goons are jailed, and at least one townsperson remains, then the townspeople win. If at this point all townspeople are jailed and at least one goon remains, then the goons win. Each evening, if there is at least one goon and at least one townsperson not in jail, then one randomly selected townsperson is jailed. If at this point there are at least as many goons remaining as townspeople remaining, then the goons win. The game ends immediately after any group wins. Suppose there are initially $1001$ townspeople and two goons. What is the probability that, when the game ends, there are exactly $1000$ people in jail?

solutions.title: Parity
solutions.body:
While the game continues, each full day jails exactly two people (one in the morning, one in the evening). An even number of jailed people ($1000$) at the end means the game ended after an evening, with the goons winning. If a goon had been jailed earlier, the goons win only when at most $1$ townsperson remains, i.e. after $1000$ townspeople and $1$ goon are jailed ($1001$ people, odd). So the only way to end with $1000$ people in jail is that no goon is ever jailed: after $500$ full days, $1000$ townspeople are jailed, leaving $1$ townsperson and $2$ goons, and the goons win.

Before morning $k$ ($k=1,\dots,500$) there are $1003-2(k-1)$ unjailed people, $2$ of them goons, so the probability that no goon is chosen is $\frac{1001-2(k-1)}{1003-2(k-1)}$ (the evening jailing never hits a goon). The product telescopes: $\frac{1001}{1003}\cdot\frac{999}{1001}\cdots\frac{3}{5}=\frac{3}{1003}$.

**Answer: $\frac{3}{1003}$**

prompt: In the city of Lincoln, there is an empty jail, at least two townspeople and at least one goon. A game proceeds over several days, starting with morning. Each morning, one randomly selected unjailed person is placed in jail. If at this point all goons are jailed, and at least one townsperson remains, then the townspeople win. If at this point all townspeople are jailed and at least one goon remains, then the goons win. Each evening, if there is at least one goon and at least one townsperson not in jail, then one randomly selected townsperson is jailed. If at this point there are at least as many goons remaining as townspeople remaining, then the goons win. The game ends immediately after any group wins. Suppose that there are initially eight townspeople and one goon. One of the eight townspeople is named Jester. If Jester is sent to jail during some morning, then the game ends immediately in his sole victory. (However, the Jester does not win if he is sent to jail during some night.) Find the probability that only the Jester wins.

solutions.title: Recursion on the number of rounds
solutions.body:
Let $a_n$ be the answer when there are $2n-1$ ordinary townspeople, the Jester and one goon (so the question is $a_4$). Each round: in the morning, with probability $\frac1{2n+1}$ the Jester is jailed (Jester wins) and with probability $\frac1{2n+1}$ the goon is jailed (townspeople win, Jester does not win alone); otherwise an ordinary person is jailed (prob. $\frac{2n-1}{2n+1}$). In the evening, the Jester is jailed with probability $\frac1{2n-1}$ (and then he cannot win), otherwise one more ordinary townsperson is jailed. This gives
$$a_n=\frac1{2n+1}+\frac{2n-1}{2n+1}\cdot\frac{2n-2}{2n-1}\,a_{n-1}=\frac1{2n+1}+\frac{2n-2}{2n+1}a_{n-1}.$$
With $a_1=\frac13$ we get $a_n=\frac13$ for every $n$ (induction: $\frac1{2n+1}+\frac{2n-2}{2n+1}\cdot\frac13=\frac{3+2n-2}{3(2n+1)}=\frac13$). So the answer is $\frac13$ (verified by exact computation).

**Answer: $\frac13$**

prompt: A parabola is the set of points in the plane equidistant from a point $F$ (its focus) and a line $\ell$ (its directrix). Parabolas can be represented as polynomial equations of degree two, such as $y=x^2$. Let $P_1,P_2,P_3$ be pairwise distinct parabolas in the plane. Find the maximum possible number of intersections between two or more of the $P_i$. In other words, find the maximum number of points that can lie on two or more of the parabolas $P_i$.

solutions.title: Pairs of parabolas
solutions.body:
Two distinct parabolas intersect in at most $4$ points (each is the zero set of a quadratic polynomial in $x,y$, and five points determine at most one such conic up to scaling, so five common points would force the two equations to be proportional and the parabolas equal). Three parabolas give $3$ pairs, hence at most $3\cdot4=12$ points. The maximum $12$ is attained, e.g. by suitably rotating three parabolas so that every pair meets in $4$ distinct points, none shared by all three.

**Answer: 12**

prompt: A parabola is the set of points in the plane equidistant from a point $F$ (its focus) and a line $\ell$ (its directrix). Parabolas can be represented as polynomial equations of degree two, such as $y=x^2$. Let $\mathcal P$ be a parabola with focus $F$ and directrix $\ell$. A line through $F$ intersects $\mathcal P$ at two points $A$ and $B$. Let $D$ and $C$ be the feet of the altitudes from $A$ and $B$ onto $\ell$, respectively. Given that $AB=20$ and $CD=14$, compute the area of $ABCD$.

solutions.title: Focus-directrix definition
solutions.body:
By definition $AD=AF$ and $BC=BF$ (distance to the directrix equals distance to the focus). Since $F$ lies on segment $AB$, $AD+BC=AF+FB=AB=20$. The quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a trapezoid with parallel sides $AD\parallel BC$ (both perpendicular to $\ell$) and height $CD=14$. Its area is $\frac12(AD+BC)\cdot CD=\frac12\cdot20\cdot14=140$.

**Answer: 140**

prompt: A parabola is the set of points in the plane equidistant from a point $F$ (its focus) and a line $\ell$ (its directrix). Parabolas can be represented as polynomial equations of degree two, such as $y=x^2$. Consider the parabola consisting of the points $(x,y)$ in the real plane satisfying $$(y+x)=(y-x)^2+3(y-x)+3.$$ Find the minimum possible value of $y$.

solutions.title: Substitute w = y - x
solutions.body:
Let $w=y-x$. Adding $w$ to both sides gives $2y=w^2+4w+3$ (since $y+x+y-x=2y$), so $y=\frac{w^2+4w+3}{2}=\frac{(w+2)^2-1}{2}$. This is minimized at $w=-2$, giving $y=-\frac12$. (Any real $w$ is attainable by choosing $x=y-w$.)

**Answer: $-\frac12$**

prompt: A parabola is the set of points in the plane equidistant from a point $F$ (its focus) and a line $\ell$ (its directrix). Parabolas can be represented as polynomial equations of degree two, such as $y=x^2$. In equilateral triangle $ABC$ with side length $2$, let the parabola with focus $A$ and directrix $BC$ intersect sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $A_1$ and $A_2$, respectively. Similarly, let the parabola with focus $B$ and directrix $CA$ intersect sides $BC$ and $BA$ at $B_1$ and $B_2$, respectively. Finally, let the parabola with focus $C$ and directrix $AB$ intersect sides $CA$ and $CB$ at $C_1$ and $C_2$, respectively. Find the perimeter of the triangle formed by lines $A_1A_2$, $B_1B_2$, $C_1C_2$.

solutions.title: Locate the points
solutions.body:
On side $AB$, the point $A_1$ of the parabola with focus $A$ and directrix $BC$ satisfies $AA_1=\operatorname{dist}(A_1,BC)=A_1B\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}A_1B$. With $AA_1+A_1B=2$ this gives $AA_1=\frac{2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{2+\sqrt3}=4\sqrt3-6=:d\approx0.928$. By symmetry each parabola meets the two sides at its focus at distance $d$ from the focus. On $AB$ the points occur in the order $A,A_1,B_2,B$ with $AA_1=BB_2=d$ and $A_1B_2=2-2d$.

The lines $A_1A_2\parallel BC$, $B_1B_2\parallel CA$, $C_1C_2\parallel AB$ form an equilateral triangle. The lines $A_1A_2$ and $B_1B_2$ meet at a point $P$ just outside $ABC$ across side $AB$, forming an equilateral triangle $PA_1B_2$ of side $2-2d$ (angles $60^\circ$ at $A_1$ and $B_2$). Similarly for the other two sides. Along the line $A_1A_2$ (of length $A_1A_2=d$, because $AA_1A_2$ is equilateral) the formed triangle's side therefore extends $2-2d$ beyond each of $A_1$ and $A_2$, so its side length is $d+2(2-2d)=4-3d=22-12\sqrt3=2(11-6\sqrt3)$. The perimeter is $3\cdot(22-12\sqrt3)=66-36\sqrt3\approx3.646$.

**Answer: $66-36\sqrt3$**

prompt: A parabola is the set of points in the plane equidistant from a point $F$ (its focus) and a line $\ell$ (its directrix). Parabolas can be represented as polynomial equations of degree two, such as $y=x^2$. Let $z$ be a complex number and $k$ a positive integer such that $z^k$ is a positive real number other than $1$. Let $f(n)$ denote the real part of the complex number $z^n$. Assume the parabola $p(n)=an^2+bn+c$ intersects $f(n)$ four times, at $n=0,1,2,3$. Assuming the smallest possible value of $k$, find the largest possible value of $a$.

solutions.title: Third finite difference
solutions.body:
Four values lie on a quadratic exactly when the third finite difference vanishes: $f(3)-3f(2)+3f(1)-f(0)=0$. Write $z=re^{i\theta}$ and $C=\cos\theta$; since $z^k>0$, $\theta=\frac{2\pi j}{k}$ with $\gcd(j,k)=1$ for minimal $k$. Then $f(n)=r^n\cos n\theta$ and the condition becomes $r^3(4C^3-3C)-1=3\bigl(r^2(2C^2-1)-rC\bigr)$.

Test small $k$. $k=1$ ($C=1$): $(r-1)^3=0$, so $r=1$ and $z^k=1$, not allowed. $k=2$ ($C=-1$): $(r+1)^3=0$, impossible for $r>0$. $k=3$ ($C=-\frac12$): $(r-1)(r+\frac12)(r+2)=0$, so $r=1$ again, not allowed. $k=4$ ($C=0$): $-1=-3r^2$, so $r=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, valid ($z^4=\frac19\ne1$). So the smallest $k$ is $4$, with $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=0$, $f(2)=-r^2=-\frac13$.

The parabola through $n=0,1,2$ has leading coefficient $a=\frac{f(0)-2f(1)+f(2)}{2}=\frac{1-\frac13}{2}=\frac13$. (For $k=4$ the value of $C$ is always $0$, so this is the only value, and hence also the largest.)

**Answer: $\frac13$**
